clue.text: No judge goes along with country yokel, ultimately

indicators.note: the pieces travel along one after another, joined end to end

parts.note: a referee, REF for short, judges a match
the USA is a country

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word yokel

explanation.surface: A judge, accompanied by a rustic from the nation, says no to something.
explanation.definitionFit: A refusal is a no, a negative response to a request or offer.

clue.text: Roger, Sussex town member speaking

indicators.note: speaking means the words are heard rather than read, so spoken they give another spelling

parts.note: Rye is a small historic town in East Sussex; a toe is a member, a limb or part of the body

explanation.surface: Someone named Roger, from a Sussex town, is a member giving a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: In radio talk 'Roger' means message received, an agreement like 'all right' or 'okay'.

clue.text: Disturbed something on phone when placing in opening of trousers

indicators.note: placing in puts the phone item inside the trouser opening

parts.note: the fly is the opening at the front of trousers
an app is an application on a smartphone

explanation.surface: Someone is upset to find something on their phone as they put it into their trouser front.
explanation.definitionFit: Flappy is informal for agitated or flustered, as in getting into a flap.

clue.text: Top sportsman, in a flash, locks vehicle

indicators.note: in places the sportsman inside the short moment

parts.note: a sec, short for second, is a flash, an instant
a dan is a top grade in judo or karate, so a master
locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: A star athlete quickly locks up a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks' looks like a verb but is the noun for hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan chair is an enclosed seat carried on poles by bearers, an old form of conveyance.

clue.text: Just army officer patrols here in Calais

indicators.note: patrols means goes around, so the officer's letters surround the French word

parts.note: Lt is short for lieutenant
ici is French for here

explanation.surface: Only an army officer keeps watch here in the French port of Calais.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit means lawful or permissible, and just in the sense of fair and legitimate.

clue.text: Quiet character in Casualty who has his sentence interrupted

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for quiet

indicators.note: in places the part played inside the hospital department

parts.note: A and E, accident and emergency, is the British hospital casualty department
a character an actor plays is a role

explanation.surface: A softly spoken part in the TV hospital drama Casualty goes to someone whose speech gets cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Casualty is also a long-running BBC hospital drama, which steers the reader towards acting; here it stands for A&E, the casualty ward.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner let out early on licence has the jail sentence interrupted, a witty play on sentence as a line of speech.

clue.text: Shark? Look round for it swimming

indicators.note: round means the look piece wraps around the mixed letters

parts.note: to peer is to look closely

indicators.note: swimming means the letters swirl about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A shark: watch out for it in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shark?' looks like the fish, which 'swimming' supports, but the question mark marks the slang sense of an exploiter.
explanation.definitionFit: Shark is slang for a swindler who exploits others, much like one making excessive gains from scarcity.

clue.text: Wanton reducing wrong when making thickener

indicators.note: reducing means cutting down, so the word for a wanton loses its tail

parts.note: a roué is a debauched, wanton man
an X marks something wrong

explanation.surface: A cook makes a sauce thicker by boiling it down after a careless mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reducing' is a kitchen word, suiting the surface, but here it cuts the last letter from ROUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A roux, cooked flour and butter, is used to thicken sauces.

clue.text: Sloth, lust, envy, anger haunting all those heartlessly criminal?

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent out of shape, so the gathered letters are rearranged
all those heartlessly means each of the four words loses its middle, keeping only the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A list of the deadly sins dogging those wicked souls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all those heartlessly' cuts LUST, ENVY, ANGER, HAUNTING to LT, EY, AR, HG, and 'criminal' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloth is laziness, and lethargy is a similar lack of energy, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Organ authorised newsman to see what worker has done at last?

definitions.text: what worker has done at last?

parts.note: the eye is an organ of sight
let means allowed, permitted
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: An organ allows a journalist to watch a labourer finish the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at last' sounds like 'finally', but a last is the foot-shaped block a shoemaker works on.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoemaker punches lace holes in a shoe on the last, the footwear mould, so it is fitted with lace holes.

clue.text: Great Dane to illustrate contest with jumps

parts.note: grand means great or impressive
a Dane is given as an example of a citizen of a country, a national

explanation.surface: A huge dog is used to depict a showjumping competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Dane' reads as the dog breed, but the words split: Great gives GRAND, and a Dane is an instance of a national.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand National is the famous British steeplechase at Aintree, a horse race over fences.

clue.text: Vacated table after having game and potato cake

indicators.note: after having places the emptied table piece behind the game

parts.note: croquet is a lawn game played with mallets and hoops

indicators.note: vacated means emptied, so only the outer letters of the word table remain

explanation.surface: Someone clears the table after a game and has a potato cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A croquette is a small fried cake of mashed potato, often breadcrumbed.

clue.text: What chef might do to skin of pheasant, with trouble

parts.note: taken as written
the outside letters of the word pheasant are P and T, the joining word spelt out in full
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A cook prepares a game bird by dealing with its skin, which proves troublesome.
explanation.walkthrough: The outside of pheasant is read as the phrase 'P and T', with the word AND written out; 'with' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooks trim the ends off vegetables such as beans or gooseberries, which is the kitchen idiom for removing both extremities.

clue.text: Plant two creatures in the hands of B. Diddley's associate

indicators.note: in the hands of means held within, so the creatures sit inside the musician's name

parts.note: Bo Diddley's fellow rock'n'roll pioneer was Chuck Berry, C. Berry
two animals: an ape and a goose

explanation.surface: Two animals are held by the rock'n'roller Bo Diddley's sidekick.
explanation.walkthrough: Bo Diddley and Chuck Berry were rock'n'roll guitarists of the 1950s; the initial-and-surname form signals C. BERRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cape gooseberry, or physalis, is a plant grown for its small orange fruit in a papery husk.

clue.text: See 12
I clean house vigorously including back of ageing furniture

indicators.note: including means the rearranged letters hold the extra piece within them
doing something vigorously stirs things up, so the letters are thrown into a new order
back of points to the final letter of the word ageing

explanation.surface: Someone cleans the house energetically, old furniture included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vigorously' rearranges I CLEAN HOUSE, and 'including' places G, the back of 'ageing', within that mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaise longue is a long upholstered sofa with a backrest at one end, an item of furniture.

clue.text: No clearance after Nigel blasted corner

indicators.note: after puts the no and clearance pieces behind the rearranged name
blasted means blown apart, so the name's letters are scattered and reformed

parts.note: OK means approval or clearance

explanation.surface: Without permission, a furious Nigel cornered someone.
explanation.definitionFit: An inglenook is a nook beside a large open fireplace, a cosy corner of a room.

clue.text: One challenging dealer maybe, as clubs trumps hearts

indicators.note: clubs beating hearts means the letter for clubs takes the place of the letter for hearts

parts.note: a dealer at cards may be one who mixes the pack

explanation.surface: At a card table a player takes on the dealer, with clubs as trumps over hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: In card notation C stands for clubs and H for hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: A scuffler is one who fights or tussles, so one offering a challenge in a scrap.

clue.text: See 9
London area supplying tea and OXO, mostly?

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: mostly means not all of it, so the final shape of the three is lost

parts.note: the letters O, X, O look like a ring, a cross and a ring

explanation.surface: A district in London provides tea and the stock cube Oxo.
explanation.walkthrough: OXO is a British brand of stock cube; here it is read as shapes. 'mostly' drops the last of the three, leaving RING CROSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Charing Cross is a district in central London, with a mainline railway station of that name.

clue.text: Quarrel almost over tweeting chat?

parts.note: a jar is a disagreement, a quarrel

indicators.note: almost means short of the full word, so the final letter goes

parts.note: gone means past, over

explanation.surface: An argument nearly finished, then carried on as tweets online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tweeting' suggests Twitter, but the old sense of jargon was the twittering of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Jargon originally meant the warbling chatter of birds, before it came to mean specialist talk.

clue.text: One propels bike, caught in traffic

indicators.note: caught means heard by the ear, so the bike part gives a word spoken the same

parts.note: a pedal drives a bicycle

explanation.surface: A cyclist gets stuck in heavy traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'traffic' reads as cars on the road, but it is the verb meaning to deal in goods.
explanation.definitionFit: To traffic is to trade, often illicitly, just as to hawk or sell goods.

clue.text: Alcoholic mixture fellow added to sauce

indicators.note: added to joins the two pieces end to end

parts.note: sauce means cheek or impudence, as does lip

explanation.surface: A man pours something into a sauce to make a boozy concoction.
explanation.definitionFit: A flip is a mixed drink of beaten egg with spirits, wine or beer, sweetened and spiced.

clue.text: Steadfast churchman redirected scamp in casualwear

indicators.note: redirected means sent the other way, so the abbreviated churchman runs backwards

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is a clergyman

indicators.note: in places the scamp inside the shirt

parts.note: a tee, or T-shirt, is casual clothing
a brat is a mischievous child, a scamp

explanation.surface: A loyal vicar is steered towards a rascal dressed in jeans and T-shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steadfast' is a figurative definition: an animal with a spine has backbone, which in people means firmness of resolve.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a backbone means showing firmness of character, so a creature with a spine is figuratively firm and resolute.

clue.text: Rock enthusiast describes banks of Wharfe river

indicators.note: describes in the sense of drawing a line around, so the enthusiast encloses the river's banks

parts.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British rock'n'roll fan

indicators.note: banks are the outer edges, so the first and last letters of the name Wharfe

explanation.surface: A rock fan portrays the edges of a Yorkshire river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wharfe is a Yorkshire river; Teds were 1950s British youths devoted to rock'n'roll.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tweed is a river along the border between England and Scotland.

clue.text: Superhuman of war getting spoils

definitions.meaning: the Roman god of battle, a deity being more than human
spoils as a verb, ruins or blemishes

explanation.surface: A god of battle collecting plunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars is the Roman god of war, and to mar is to spoil, so the third person form fits spoils.

clue.text: Old tenor heading off composed somewhere in the Atlantic

parts.note: Mario Lanza was a mid-twentieth-century American tenor and film star

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed from the word for composed

parts.note: to have composed music or text is to have written it

explanation.surface: A former tenor sets off and composed a piece somewhere out at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Lanzarote is one of the Canary Islands, lying in the Atlantic Ocean off north-west Africa.

clue.text: Firm's free to employ serviceman

indicators.note: to employ is to take on, so the free piece takes the soldier inside it

parts.note: to rid is to free or clear
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A company is at liberty to hire an ex-soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm's' reads as a company's possession, but it is 'Firm is', an adjective meaning stiff.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigid and firm are synonyms, both meaning stiff and not bending.

clue.text: The Parisian to get fine after game? Writing on the wall perhaps

indicators.note: after places the French article and the fine piece behind the game

parts.note: RU is rugby union
les is the French plural for the
OK means fine or all right

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is told all will be well after a match, like a sign on a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Graffiti in Britain often took the form 'Arsenal rules OK', a boast scrawled on walls.

clue.text: Yvette's outside captivated by poet she's respected highly

indicators.note: captivated by means held captive inside, so the outer letters sit within the poet

parts.note: John Donne was an English metaphysical poet

indicators.note: outside means only the first and last letters of the name Yvette are used

explanation.surface: Yvette's exterior charm wins over a poet who esteems her greatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyenne is the most senior or eminent woman in a field, held in high regard.
